t.1.5.1: This whole earth, from the very first, belonged to those victorious kings, beginning with Prajāpati.
t.1.5.3: This great narrative, known as the Rāmāyaṇa, arose in the lineage of those great-souled kings, the Ikṣvākus.
t.1.5.2: Of their line was the one named Sagara, by whom the ocean was caused to be dug, and whom sixty thousand sons surrounded as he went forth.
t.1.5.4: I shall now relate this whole account in its entirety from the beginning. Joined with dharma, kāma and artha, it should be heard without envy.
t.1.5.5: There is a great country named Kosala, joyful and prosperous, settled on the bank of the Sarayū, abounding in wealth and grain.
t.1.5.6: There was a city named Ayodhyā, renowned throughout the world, a city that Manu, the lord of men, had built himself.
t.1.5.7: That great city, glorious and splendid, extended twelve yojanas in length and three in breadth, with its great highways well laid out.
t.1.5.8: It was adorned by a great royal highway, well laid out, strewn with scattered flowers and constantly sprinkled with water.
t.1.5.9: King Daśaratha, enlarger of the great kingdom, inhabited that city, just as the lord of the gods dwells in heaven.
t.1.5.10: A city furnished with doors and arched gateways, with well-laid-out markets within, stocked with every kind of machine and weapon, and inhabited by artisans of every craft.
t.1.5.12: And the great city was filled on every side with troupes of women actors and dancers, furnished with gardens and mango groves, and girdled by a rampart of sāla trees as by a belt.
t.1.5.11: The city was thronged with sūtas and māgadhas, glorious and of matchless splendor, with lofty watchtowers flying banners, and bristling with hundreds of śataghnīs.
t.1.5.13: The city had deep, impassable moats and was a fortress that others could not assail; it was filled with horses and elephants, and likewise with cattle, camels and donkeys.
t.1.5.14: The city was thronged by hosts of vassal kings with their offerings of tribute, and adorned by merchants who dwelt there from many different lands.
t.1.5.15: It was adorned with jewel-wrought palaces that rose like mountains, and filled with many-storied pavilions, like Indra's Amarāvatī.
t.1.5.16: That wondrous city, laid out like a chessboard, thronged with hosts of excellent women, strewn with every kind of jewel, and adorned with palatial mansions.
t.1.5.18: That city, unsurpassed upon the earth, resounded loudly and exceedingly with kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās and paṇavas.
t.1.5.17: The city was densely packed with houses, leaving no gaps, and built on level ground. It was filled with grains of śāli rice, and its water was as sweet as the juice of sugarcane.
t.1.5.19: The city was like a celestial chariot of the Siddhas, won in heaven through austerity, its houses well arranged throughout, and it was thronged with the finest of men.
t.1.5.20: And they, deft of hand and skilled, do not pierce with their arrows one who stands alone and has no one behind him, nor a distant target that can be struck only by sound.
t.1.5.21: They are slayers of lions, tigers and boars that roam maddened and roaring in the forest, killing them with sharpened weapons, and even by sheer force with the strength of their bare arms.
t.1.5.22: King Daśaratha then inhabited that city, filled with thousands of such great chariot-warriors.
t.1.5.23: That city was thronged with the foremost of the twice-born, keepers of the sacred fires, rich in virtue, masters of the Vedas and their six limbs, givers of thousands, devoted to truth, great-souled men who were like great sages, and with true sages as well.
